Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

name.description: Name for the spawned agent. Makes it addressable via SendMessage({to: name}) while running.

team_name.description: Deprecated; ignored. The session has a single implicit team.

mode.description: Deprecated; ignored. Subagents inherit the parent session's permission mode; agent-definition frontmatter may override it.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__edit_version
tools.description: Publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit (some clients refuse any artifact but your own as owner-only), by replacing text in its current document: use it for a small change instead of sending the whole page to publish_version. The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. Each old_text must occur exactly once in the document as it stands when that edit is applied: include enough surrounding text to make it unique. base_version must name the live version (from get_artifact, read_artifact, list_files or your last publish result); if it is no longer live the call is rejected with a conflict that names the live version: read what you are changing again and retry. To rename the artifact pass title, which also rewrites the document's <title> element; an edit to that element without title is refused, because the server keeps it in step with the artifact's title. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document cannot be edited here. An artifact made from a type is edited only if this server offers list_files, and only with path: one of its own text files, as list_files lists them, never its page or its type's files.

tools.description: List artifacts in your organization that you can open: your own, then those shared with you or that you have viewed, most recent first; with shared_only, only the latter. tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_files
tools.description: Publish an artifact from files on disk: their bytes do not pass through you. Prefer this to publish_version when the page's files already exist, when there is more than one file or an image, or when the page is large. For each file give `as`, the path it is served at, and `path`, its absolute path on the machine where your own file tools run; leave `uri` out. index.html is required in a new artifact. Limits for one call: 256 files, 20 MiB a file, 64 MiB in all. The client may refuse a file it will not send, such as a secrets file, a link or a path outside the working folder. Omit slug to create an artifact, private to you. To republish, give slug and base_version (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish); title and icon are kept when omitted. Past 256 files, send the rest in later republishes. A republish changes only the files named and keeps the rest, which stay served: to take a file away, list it in remove. mode "replace" makes the files named the whole artifact and drops the rest. This tool publishes only to an artifact of yours. **Files Claude did not write**: Claude reads the whole file before publishing it, even when the person asks it not to. Publishing distributes the content, and Claude never distributes what it has not seen. A request for privacy is a reason to read before publishing, not an exemption. If Claude cannot read the file, it does not publish it. **Claude never publishes** a page that impersonates a real person or organization, for example by using their name, branding, byline or domain. Claude also never publishes fabricated records, receipts or reviews presented as genuine, forms or flows that collect credentials or payment details under false pretenses, or content that targets a private individual. Claude refuses whether it wrote the page or the person supplied it, and whatever purpose is claimed, such as a prop or a test, when the page would work as the real thing. If publishing is refused, Claude does not suggest other ways to host or share the page.

tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__publish_version
tools.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. Some clients may publish only to your own artifacts: there the call is refused as owner-only. Republishing is read-then-send: base_version must name the live version you are replacing (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result) — if it is no longer live, the publish is rejected with a conflict; re-read and retry from the current state. On success the new version goes live immediately. When republishing, the artifact's stored connectors manifest carries forward unchanged, and so do title, favicon, icon and contract when omitted. schema.description: Publish an artifact: either create a new artifact — omit slug and give title and content; you become its owner and it starts private to you — or publish a new version of an artifact you own, or of one in your organization that you can edit — give slug and base_version. Some clients may publish only to your own artifacts: there the call is refused as owner-only. Republishing is read-then-send: base_version must name the live version you are replacing (from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result) — if it is no longer live, the publish is rejected with a conflict; re-read and retry from the current state. On success the new version goes live immediately. When republishing, the artifact's stored connectors manifest carries forward unchanged, and so do title, favicon, icon and contract when omitted. Content is capped at 16 MiB.

artifact_title.description: The artifact's current title, as get_artifact gives it. Needed when shared_live is 'public'.

base_version.description: Required when slug is given: the version id this publish replaces — echo the version get_artifact or read_artifact returned (or your last publish result's). Rejected with a conflict if it no longer names the live version, so concurrent edits are never silently overwritten. Omit when creating.

content.description: The complete HTML document, at most 16 MiB. Must sniff as text/html — begin it with <!DOCTYPE html>.

contract.description: Optional runtime-contract version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Leave it out to keep the current one. Pass one only when the user asks for a different version, or this server's answer says to. If the publish is rejected because the contract is yanked or out of the supported window, republish with an explicit "0.0.0" to clear the contract — omitting the argument is not a reliable recovery (the server may carry the stored contract forward, repeating the rejection).

deadline.description: Optional, rarely needed: by when pages still open on an OLDER version must have moved to this one — one word: now, 15m, 1h, 24h, 7d, or an ISO-8601 time at most 30 days ahead. Omit it for ordinary edits (open pages then move at their next quiet moment); it cannot be relaxed once published.

favicon.description: Optional legacy emoji marker; omit it.

icon.description: One short, generic word for the artifact's tab icon — a plain signifier of what it is, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map; not a product or brand name. Pass one when creating; omit when republishing to keep the current icon.

shared_live.description: States who the artifact you are republishing is already shared with, and changes nothing: its 'read' value from get_artifact, read_artifact or your last publish result. Required when that value is 'users' (named people or groups), 'org' (the user's whole organization) or 'public' (anyone with the link). Leave it out for a new artifact and when the value is 'owner'. slug.description: The artifact's server-assigned slug (UUID), e.g. from list_artifacts, get_artifact or the artifact's own URL. Omit to create a new artifact.

title.description: Browser-tab title. Required when creating. When republishing it is optional — omitted, the new version keeps the current live version's title (the server also keeps the stored HTML's <title> element in sync with it); pass a value only to rename the artifact, never invent a new title on a routine republish.

content.content:
# Joe

## Who

Joe, born 18 Jun 1989, 172 cm. Desk job, doesn't drive, walks for errands. Intermediate:
one to three years of structured training. Logs every lift in Hevy (Pro), runs with Runna on a
Garmin watch, weighs in each morning on a Garmin Index scale, and tracks food in MacroFactor.

## Goal and phase

Size and raw strength for the whole body, with no gaps: strong arms, shoulders, chest, core and
legs, the strongman or powerbuilder look, at a body fat that is easy to live at (about
15–18 %). The test is jeans and a t-shirt, not abs at any cost. The five fundamental compounds
lead: strict pull-up, bench press, overhead press, deadlift and back squat (box squats are a
fine variation). Accessory work exists to support them and to build a strong, healthy body.
Long-term targets: five strict pull-ups, bench 1.25×BW, OHP 0.75×BW, deadlift 2×BW, squat
1.5×BW.

Body fat is about 25–27 %. The phase is maintenance for the first weeks on this program, while
training and logging food and weight become regular. Then a small deficit (about 0.3 % of
bodyweight a week) leans out without giving up strength or size. A lean bulk follows once the look says about 20 % body fat, judged by waist and photos at
a deep check-in, never by a date. After that, the plan is to move between a floor of about
15–16 % and a ceiling of about 20–22 % for years while strength and muscle build. MacroFactor
sets the calories; protein aim 175 g a day.

Joe wants one or two strength-conditioning sessions a week, like the old program's kettlebell
and circuit sessions, and is open to redesigning them.

## The week and why it has its shape

Six training days, resting Thursday. The Tuesday evening session is with a personal trainer at
the gym; the PT programmes it and Joe does not control its content. It alternates chest and
back (bench, lat pulldowns, curls) with legs and core (back or box squat, sometimes deadlifts,
core). The other five days are home sessions.

Three easy runs a week (Wednesday lunchtime, Saturday, Sunday), set by Runna, share days with
home lifting. Wednesday's lift is in the morning, before the run.

Weekday sessions are capped at about 75 minutes, weekends at about 90.

Home is Ironmaster Quick-Lock kit on one shared plate pool: bar, two dumbbells, kettlebell, leg
attachment and a weighted vest (up to 30 kg, not yet in use). Ironmaster bench (flat and
incline) with pull-up bar and dip station, a box, bands and rings. No machines or cables at
home. The home bar tops out at 228 lb, which caps squat and deadlift there. Joe can use the gym
outside the PT session when needed: for heavy singles and test singles, and for squat and
deadlift work near the cap. When a squat or deadlift top set reaches about 220 lb, that lift
moves to the gym. Until then the working squat and deadlift stay at home.

## Body and limits

Nothing limiting as of 1 Nov 2026. Sleep has been the limiter since August: missed sessions
trace to late nights, and bedtime is the lever. Smart-scale body fat is a trend, not a number:
same scale, morning, fasted.

## How Joe wants to be coached

- A bad night moves the session to the evening or the next free day; it doesn't cancel it.
- Waist and body fat are a monthly ask at deep check-ins only. Weekly asks go unanswered.
- Direct biceps work is dumbbell curls, not barbell.
- Pull-ups and dips build through negatives first, banded volume second (progress by shrinking
  the band, not chasing reps) and hangs on long days. Strict sets become real work once the
  test rep passes about five.

## History before this system

Trained with the first coach from 19 Jul 2026 after a four-week layoff, then its rewrite from
13 Oct 2026. The six-day plan landed about half the time, lost mostly to late nights and two

# Joe

## Who

Joe, born 18 Jun 1989, 172 cm. Desk job, doesn't drive, walks for errands. Intermediate:
one to three years of structured training. Logs every lift in Hevy (Pro), runs with Runna on a
Garmin watch, weighs in each morning on a Garmin Index scale, and tracks food in MacroFactor.

## Goal and phase

Size and raw strength for the whole body, with no gaps: strong arms, shoulders, chest, core and
legs, the strongman or powerbuilder look, at a body fat that is easy to live at (about
15–18 %). The test is jeans and a t-shirt, not abs at any cost. The five fundamental compounds
lead: strict pull-up, bench press, overhead press, deadlift and back squat (box squats are a
fine variation). Accessory work exists to support them and to build a strong, healthy body.
Long-term targets: five strict pull-ups, bench 1.25×BW, OHP 0.75×BW, deadlift 2×BW, squat
1.5×BW.

Body fat is about 25–27 %. The phase is maintenance for the first weeks on this program, while
training and logging food and weight become regular. Then a small deficit (about 0.3 % of
bodyweight a week) leans out without giving up strength or size. A lean bulk follows once the look says about 20 % body fat, judged by waist and photos at
a deep check-in, never by a date. After that, the plan is to move between a floor of about
15–16 % and a ceiling of about 20–22 % for years while strength and muscle build. MacroFactor
sets the calories; protein aim 175 g a day.

Joe wants one or two strength-conditioning sessions a week, like the old program's kettlebell
and circuit sessions, and is open to redesigning them.

## The week and why it has its shape

Six training days, resting Thursday. The Tuesday evening session is with a personal trainer at
the gym; the PT programmes it and Joe does not control its content. It alternates chest and
back (bench, lat pulldowns, curls) with legs and core (back or box squat, sometimes deadlifts,
core). The other five days are home sessions.

Three easy runs a week (Wednesday lunchtime, Saturday, Sunday), set by Runna, share days with
home lifting. Wednesday's lift is in the morning, before the run.

Weekday sessions are capped at about 75 minutes, weekends at about 90.

Home is Ironmaster Quick-Lock kit on one shared plate pool: bar, two dumbbells, kettlebell, leg
attachment and a weighted vest (up to 30 kg, not yet in use). Ironmaster bench (flat and
incline) with pull-up bar and dip station, a box, bands and rings. No machines or cables at
home. The home bar tops out at 228 lb, which caps squat and deadlift there. Joe can use the gym
outside the PT session when needed: for heavy singles and test singles, and for squat and
deadlift work near the cap. When a squat or deadlift top set reaches about 220 lb, that lift
moves to the gym. Until then the working squat and deadlift stay at home.

## Body and limits

Nothing limiting as of 1 Nov 2026. Sleep has been the limiter since August: missed sessions
trace to late nights, and bedtime is the lever. Smart-scale body fat is a trend, not a number:
same scale, morning, fasted.

## How Joe wants to be coached

- A bad night moves the session to the evening or the next free day; it doesn't cancel it.
- Waist and body fat are a monthly ask at deep check-ins only. Weekly asks go unanswered.
- Direct biceps work is dumbbell curls, not barbell.
- Pull-ups and dips build through negatives first, banded volume second (progress by shrinking
  the band, not chasing reps) and hangs on long days. Strict sets become real work once the
  test rep passes about five.

## History before this system

Trained with the first coach from 19 Jul 2026 after a four-week layoff, then its rewrite from
13 Oct 2026. The six-day plan landed about half the time, lost mostly to late nights and two
illnesses. Moved to this engine on 1 Nov 2026 with a fresh program.

| `superset` | no | A label; lines sharing it in one session are performed together |

### Set group

| Key | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | yes | Sets in the group |
| `type` | no, default `working` | `warm_up`, `working`, `activation`, `test` |
| `reps` | reps-based | An integer, a range `[6, 8]`, or an open top `"8+"` for a rep-out |
| `duration_s` | duration lines | Instead of `reps` |
| `rpe` | per the registry | Required on every working group of a scheme whose rule reads it (`double_progression`, `linear`, `assistance_ladder`) and on the top group of `top_backoff`; missing is `rpe_missing`. Optional elsewhere (a back-off, a `hold` line, `wave_531`), where it is rendered and never a ceiling. Stored as RPE; a hypertrophy line renders it as RIR (`10 − rpe`). Never filled: the `program` skill proposes it from `goals.md`'s band |

Set types:

- `warm_up` groups carry `count` and `reps` only; their loads are derived from the first working
  set's load by the registry ramp and the ADR 0008 ladder (`prescription.md`, Warm-ups) and never
  authored.
- `working` is the default. Sets to failure are working sets; a rep-out is a working group with
  an open top.
- `activation` is a real type: low load, counts no hard set, excluded from e1RM and from the
  working-set count. A line whose only groups are activation is valid and yields no Exposure
  (the old "warm-up with no working sets" problem, review "The data model").
- `test` is the heavy single the deload policy prescribes on a priority lift in the light week,
  whose result the coach may record as the next block's training max (a `training_max` Decision,
  ADR 0016). It is never authored: a `test` group in the Draft is `set_type_not_allowed`. A
  weekly max attempt is a `working` single.

Set structures (drop sets, rest-pause, myo-reps) are not in v1. The evidence puts them level with
straight sets for growth and ahead only on time (`rn:progression-methods §1`), no source uses one
as a stall response, and the four set types cannot express them: a group would need its own
rest, a load taken from the group before it, and a rule for which of its sets count as hard
sets and qualify for e1RM. A version that wants one authors plain working sets. When they
arrive, the opening set of a myo-rep cluster is a `working` set, so `activation` keeps its
meaning.

### Dose and deload

Both are version tables so that `prescribe` reads the version, never the Goal or the Phase.
Absent, adopt fills them from the emphasis and the open Phase (`goals.md`, "Defaults per
emphasis") and the dry run shows the filled values. Present, they stand and may draw
`dose_off_band` or `deload_off_emphasis`. With a lifting session's `minutes`, these are the only
things adopt fills: a line's scheme, RPE and rest are coaching judgement the `program` skill
authors, and adopt warns where they sit outside the emphasis band.

```toml
[dose]
per_muscle = 10          # hard sets per muscle per week
[dose.lift]
bb_bench_press = 8       # one entry per priority lift
pull_up = { sets = 8, counts = ["negative_pull_up", "band_pull_up"] }

[deload]
hard_weeks_ceiling = 6   # the Block ceiling; was `blocks.hard_weeks_ceiling`
set_cut_pct = 40         # off each working group's sets in the light week
load_cut_pct = 0         # off the working load; the evidence keeps the load (rn:goal-programming §6)
rpe_cap = 8              # ceiling on every set in the light week
test_priority_lifts = true
```

The three shape fields are the light cut `prescription.md` applies on every lifting line of a
`light_week`; the override may restate any of them for one week (`overrides.md`).

A `[dose.lift]` entry is a bare target, or a table whose `sets` is the target and whose `counts`
names the lift's counted variants: exercises whose hard sets add to the lift's weekly figure,
one each, under the same exposure filter as the per-muscle dose (`week.md`, "Dose"). A lift
trained mostly through its rungs (a strict pull-up built with negatives and band pull-ups) keeps
a target inside the band this way. Adopt never fills `counts`; choosing a lift's variants is
coaching judgement. The variants count toward the target and the disrupted-week floor only:
they do not stand in for the lift on a line (`priority_lift_absent`), are never tested, and
need not come first in a session. `dose_off_band` reads `sets`.

### New exercises

A line references an Exercise by library id. The engine ships its catalogue as seed data the
store imports at `init`; the instance's library is the store's `exercise` table and nothing
else. A new exercise is declared in the same Draft and upserted in adopt's transaction:

```toml
[exercise.custom_ring_push_up]
name = "Ring push-up"
load_mode = "bodyweight"
equipment_kind = "bodyweight"
pattern = "horizontal_push"
muscles = { primary = ["chest"], secondary = ["triceps", "front_delts"] }
# without a Hevy template id, the four template columns (ADR 0011):
hevy_title = "Ring Push Up"
hevy_exercise_type = "reps_only"
hevy_equipment = "other"
hevy_muscle_group = "chest"
```

A declared exercise that already exists is updated field by field; `hevy_template_id` is never
set here (it is written by `plan apply` after a verified create, ADR 0011).

### Acknowledgements

The same shape as the plan Draft's (`validation.md`, "Leaving a warning"). Adopt freezes them on
the version; an entry whose key adopt did not raise is a violation so a stale acknowledgement
cannot ride along.

name = "Ring push-up"
load_mode = "bodyweight"
equipment_kind = "bodyweight"

One shape, no rule plugins. `rotation` is an ordered list of week names; each named table maps
weekdays to a session id or a non-empty list of session ids. A one-week rotation is the old
`fixed_weekdays`; a coach-led session that anchors the week is just a coach-led session on its
weekday in every rotation week.

Each entry is a slot, so a weekday may hold several sessions, of any kinds. List order is the
order within the day: the plan plans them in that order and every listing of the week shows them
in it. A one-element list and a bare id are the same schedule. A session scheduled beside another
keeps all its own fields (scheme, `minutes`, routine); nothing merges, and there is no day-level
time budget.

```toml
[schedule]
rotation = ["A", "B"]

[schedule.A]
mon = ["lower-a", "cond-swings"]
tue = "coach-led"
thu = "push-a"
sat = "pull-a"

[schedule.B]
mon = "pull-b"
tue = "coach-led"
thu = "lower-b"
sat = "push-b"
```

A session that appears in the schedule has cadence `weekly`. Standing and daily sessions declare
their cadence on the session and never appear in the schedule.

### Session

| Key | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | yes | Stable across versions: the Routine map, park and resume Decisions, matching and the hard-week count hang off it. A renamed id is a retired session plus a new one |
| `title` | yes | |
| `kind` | yes | `lifting`, `conditioning`, `practice`, `coach_led`. Never `rehab`: a rehab session is carried by its niggle (ADR 0010) |
| `tier` | yes | `core` or `optional`. A practice must be `optional` |
| `cadence` | when not in the schedule | `standing` or `daily`; a scheduled session is `weekly` and may not state a cadence |
| `location` | no | Departs from the version's default |
| `minutes` | no | The session's time budget; the rest-and-sets estimate over it is a warning. A lifting session that states none takes `[athlete].session_minutes`, filled into the version at adopt like an emphasis default |
| `scheme` | conditioning only | Session-level scheme, below |
| `estimated_sets` | coach-led only | `{ chest = 4, lats = 4, ... }` hard sets per muscle; a coach-led session has no lines |
| `[[session.line]]` | lifting, conditioning, practice | Below |

No `status`: a parked session is a Decision, not a field (ADR 0010).

### Line

A proposal **stands** until the next plan carries a `light_week` override or a `decline_ceiling`
Decision is written after it; `status` reports a standing one as "light week or deload pending".
Two triggers with no light week taken is the coach's call and raises nothing.

Per muscle, the fractional hard sets delivered in the closed week (direct 1, indirect 0.5; a
hard set is a working set above RPE 5, rn:volume-frequency.2, rn:proximity-to-failure.5) against
the version's target, and the mean over the trailing four ordinary weeks. The card carries it;
`plan draft` raises `dose_under_target` when delivered dose is under target in at least three of
the trailing four ordinary weeks (rn:volume-frequency.1; three of four is opinion) and
`session_dose_high` when a planned session exceeds 11 fractional sets (rn:volume-frequency.3). `progress` keeps its block-boundary
view.
----CONDITIONING-DOSE

## Problem

`plan apply --dry-run` cuts its `flags` list to the first 10 by default, so the agent can approve a plan without seeing every warning that is not left.

## What happens (on `build/v2`, PR #200)

The dry run's default `flags` rows are `{key, severity, left}`, cut to `--last` (10), with `flag_count` and `flags_truncated` beside them. Only `--full` shows every flag, and only `--full` carries `params_hash`. The first Draft at the 2026-11-01 cutover carried 27 flags, so the default dry run would have hidden 17.

`docs/spec/verbs.md` lets this verb run over the 6 KB budget because "their whole default output is what the agent must act on". Cutting the flag list works against that reason. #181 made `plan draft` and `query flags` show every flag and left this verb out of scope on purpose.

## Decided fix

- The dry run's default `flags` list shows every flag, uncut. Each row is `{key, code, severity, params_hash, left}`: short, but enough to write an `[[acknowledge]]` entry without a second call.
- `flag_count` stays. `flags_truncated` goes, or is always false; pick one and say which in the spec.
- The text approval prompt (`src/coach/render/approval_prompt.py`) stays as it is: ADR 0006 sets its layout at about 40 lines, with 5 items per section and a count of the rest.
- `--full` keeps its full flag documents.

202 CLOSED 2026-11-02T20:56:37Z Keep conditioning workouts out of the e1RM and progress reads, and amend ADR 0010
**Target:** build on `build/v2` (draft PR #200), not `main`: the code this changes exists only there so far. Ships in release 0.2.0, before PR #200 merges.

## Problem

ADR 0010 says a conditioning workout yields "an Activity and no Exposures". `prescription.md` says conditioning lines run `hold`, which anchors on the last Exposure. The two rules conflict, and the code now follows neither one fully.

## What happens (on `build/v2`, after #175 / PR #197)

#175 keeps a matched conditioning workout's Exposures in the shared history, so the next `cond-swings` hold line anchors on the logged swings. Without them, every swings line fell back to `start_load` each week. The closed-week dose, the check-in lift rows and the return-week lifting dates leave these workouts out (`WeekLog.exposures` and `WeekLog.conditioning` in `src/coach/services/closed_weeks.py`). The e1RM read, `coach progress`, `query exposures`, cadence and the program check still see them. So a swing logged in a conditioning session can move the e1RM, and the progress figures, of a lifting line that uses the same exercise.

## Decided fix

The owner chose to keep the anchor behaviour and amend the ADR. The rule is the same one ADR 0010 already gives practice workouts: the work feeds only its own session.

- Amend ADR 0010's "What each kind's workout yields" so the conditioning bullet reads, in substance: *A conditioning workout yields an Activity. Its sets anchor its own session's lines and nothing else: they count toward no hard sets, no muscle balance, no lifting day and no e1RM.* Fix the matching regression-test bullet ("a conditioning workout produces no Exposure") the same way.
- The e1RM read (`top_backoff`, RPE ceilings, `top_set_above_e1rm`, the carried e1RM) and `coach progress` (e1RM, stall streak, dose) leave out Exposures from workouts matched to a conditioning session.
- A conditioning session's own line history, read by exercise and session, keeps them, so hold lines still anchor on the logged sets.
- Keep `query exposures` as a raw read that shows them. Decide during triage whether it should mark them, and say so in `verbs.md`.

## Acceptance (draft, for triage to firm up)

- A kettlebell swing logged in a conditioning session doesn't change the e1RM, or the `progress` figures, of a lifting line with the same exercise.
- The next conditioning hold line still anchors on the logged sets (`derived_from` names the exposure).
- The ADR and `prescription.md` agree.

## Spec

`docs/adr/0010-sessions-outside-the-rotation.md`, `prescription.md` (the e1RM window and conditioning lines), `GLOSSARY.md` (Exposure, if its definition says otherwise), and possibly `verbs.md` (`query exposures`).

Once the issues raised from the 2026-11-01 cutover are fixed and released, bring Joe's instance (`~/personal/training`, `joeuk89/training`) onto that release and undo the workarounds the cutover needed. Each item says what to check; skip any the fix makes unnecessary.

- Install the release and run `coach upgrade` in the instance; `coach status` shows the new version equal to the pin.

- **#174 (dose variants).** Restate `[dose.lift]` so `pull_up` counts `negative_pull_up` and `band_pull_up`, with a target inside the band, and drop the `dose_off_band` acknowledgement.
- **#175 (finisher).** Move the KB swing line out of `mon-ohp` back into a conditioning session with `emom_density` (12 → 16 min, 12 → 15 reps, RPE 7), scheduled beside Monday's lifting session. Check that `dose` no longer counts the swings as hard sets.
- **#176 (standing dates).** No change to the program; check that `cond-circuit` no longer needs a weekly `session_drop_suggested` acknowledgement.

## Plan (the next `plan-week` after the release)

- **#185 (data-error anchor).** If `custom_suitcase_carry` still anchors on the 2026-05-22 load-0 exposure, set its load to the athlete's working weight (40 lb at cutover, or whatever he has logged since).
- **#173 (pre-layoff e1RM).** Check the deadlift's top set against its August history (170.5×6); remove any weekly `pin_load` and `increment_over_step` acknowledgement the workaround needed.
- **#177 (stall streaks).** Check that the old program's stall warnings are gone.

## Kit

- **joeuk89/plate-pool#52** (#183 closed without a stopgap). Once plate-pool's `achievable` command ships, regenerate `kit/home.achievable.json` with it and confirm the rows match the hand-wrapped tables (no rack change; `coach status` shows `current`). Then `publish`.

## Done when

The instance runs the new release, the program and plan carry none of the cutover workarounds above, `coach status` shows no warnings, and `publish` has committed and pushed the result.

cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-joeabousselam-personal-training/f731c80b-6c6f-4ab6-9445-2caab7bd42c5/scratchpad/issue.md <<'EOF'
## Problem

`program adopt` shows at most one `dose_off_band` per version. The dose check returns after the first off-band target, and the flag is keyed on the version alone, so a second off-band target is hidden until the first is fixed.

## What happens (0.2.0)

`WarningChecks.dose` in `src/coach/core/program/warnings.py` loops over `per_muscle` and each `[dose.lift]` target and `return`s after the first `raise_`. The scope is `version_scope`, so the key is `dose_off_band@version:pv-N` whatever the target.

Seen on Joe's instance:

- The pv-1 dry run on 2026-11-01 showed `dose_off_band` for `pull_up = 1` only. `bb_deadlift = 4` was also outside the 5–15 per-lift band and never appeared.
- The pv-2 amend on 2026-11-02 (#186, the #174 item) restated `pull_up` inside the band. The dry run then raised `dose_off_band` for `bb_deadlift = 4`, which had been off band since pv-1.

So an athlete can adopt a version with an unseen off-band target, and each later version that fixes one reveals the next. The acknowledgement on pv-1 named the pull-up, while the version also carried an unacknowledged deadlift target.

## Decided fix (proposal, for triage)

- Drop the early `return`: raise one `dose_off_band` per off-band target.
- Put the target in the key so two targets do not collide on one acknowledgement. The line-scoped flags carry the exercise; this one should carry the muscle or lift, for example `dose_off_band@version:pv-2/bb_deadlift` or a `dose` scope with the target as its id. Triage picks the shape.
- Say how a frozen acknowledgement on the old key migrates. pv-2 on Joe's instance carries `dose_off_band@version:pv-2` acknowledged for `bb_deadlift`; the next adopt under the new key must not reject it as stale (`program.md`, Acknowledgements: an entry whose key adopt did not raise is a violation) without saying what to write instead.

## Acceptance (draft)

- A Draft with `pull_up = 1` and `bb_deadlift = 4` under a 5–15 band raises two `dose_off_band` warnings in one dry run, with distinct keys.
- Acknowledging one leaves the other standing.
- `per_muscle` off band and a lift off band in the same Draft raise two flags.
- A version acknowledged under the old key adopts cleanly, or the dry run names the new key to write.

## Spec

`docs/spec/goals.md` and `docs/spec/validation.md` (the `dose_off_band` rows: scope and key), `docs/spec/program.md` ("Dose and deload", and the Acknowledgements rule if the migration needs words there).
EOF
